etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English merren, from Old English mierran (“to mar, disturb, confuse; scatter, squander, waste; upset, hinder, obstruct; err”), from Proto-Germanic *marzijaną (“to disturb, hinder”), from Proto-Indo-European *mers- (“to annoy, disturb, neglect, forget, ignore”). Cognate with Scots mer, mar (“to obstruct, impede, spoil, ruin”), Dutch marren (“to push along, delay, hinder”), dialectal German merren (“to entangle”), Icelandic merja (“to bruise, crush”), Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐍂𐌶𐌾𐌰𐌽 (marzjan, “to annoy, bother, disturb, offend”), Lithuanian miršti (“to forget, lose, become oblivious, die”), Armenian մոռանալ (moṙanal, “to forget, fail”), Sanskrit मृष् (mṛṣ, “forget, neglect”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To spoil; to ruin; to scathe; to damage.

quote.citation: 1551, William Turner, “Prologe”, in A new Herball, etc.‎[1], folio Aiiii:
quote.text: […]  and putteth ether many a good mā by ignorance in ieopardy of his life, or marreth good medicines to the great diſhoneſtie both of the Phiſician and of Goddes worthy creatures, the herbes and medecines:

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: Prospero:  […] huſh, and be mute / Or elſe our ſpell is mar'd.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, Paradise Lost. A Poem Written in Ten Books, London: Printed [by Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker under Creed Church neer Aldgate; and by Robert Boulter at the Turks Head in Bishopsgate-street; and Matthias Walker, under St. Dunstons Church in Fleet-street, →OCLC:
quote.text: Ire, envy, and despair / Marred all his borrowed visage, and betrayed / Him counterfeit.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Homer’s Ilias”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, book I, page 218:
quote.text: Mother, tho' wiſe your ſelf, my Counſel weigh; / 'Tis much unſafe my Sire to disobey; / Not only you provoke him to your Coſt, / But Mirth is marr'd, and the good Chear is loſt.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
See mere. Doublet of mare and mere.

(1175) « shallow and stagnating little body of water » from old norrois marr (« see, lake »), similar to old Saxon meri, from ancient German meri, German Meer, Anglo-Saxon mere (« swamp ; lake »).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Alternative form of mayor and mair.
